title: When you’re caught between ‘yes’ and ‘no,’ here’s why ‘maybe’ isn’t the way to go
titleZh: 当你在“去”与“不去”之间犹豫时，“再说吧”不是好答案
summary:
假设你在一次电台抽奖中，抽中了两张本周末那场早已售罄的演唱会门票。你满心欢喜地给朋友发消息，问他们是否想要一起去。结果对方只回了句：“看情况吧。”你的心情瞬间跌落。原本的喜悦变成了一种被轻视的失落，你陷入了尴尬的等待：你现在只能等这位犹豫不决的朋友作出决定，才能安排自己的演唱会计划。

来源：对话；作者：Julian Givi；原文发布时间：2025-09-09 20:00:00

paragraphs.contentEn: Say you win a radio sweepstakes giving you two tickets to a sold-out concert the upcoming weekend. You eagerly text your friend and ask if they’d like to join. Their response? “Maybe.” Your mood immediately turns. You feel slighted rather than joyous as you’re left in limbo: Now you need to wait for your waffling friend to make a decision before you can figure out your plans for the concert.
paragraphs.contentZh: 假设你在一次电台抽奖中，抽中了两张本周末那场早已售罄的演唱会门票。你满心欢喜地给朋友发消息，问他们是否想要一起去。结果对方只回了句：“看情况吧。”你的心情瞬间跌落。原本的喜悦变成了一种被轻视的失落，你陷入了尴尬的等待：你现在只能等这位犹豫不决的朋友作出决定，才能安排自己的演唱会计划。

paragraphs.contentEn: I’m a consumer psychologist who has studied social decision-making for over a decade. And if you’ve experienced anything like the above anecdote, I can tell you that you’re not alone. People responding “maybe” to invitations is a common yet irksome aspect of social life. Recently, my co-authors and I published a series of studies examining what goes on in people’s heads when they aren’t sure whether to accept an invitation.
paragraphs.contentZh: 我是一名消费心理学家，专注于社会决策行为研究已有十余年。如果你曾经历过上述类似的情境，我可以告诉你，这种情况并不罕见。在社交生活中，用“可能”来回应邀请是一种常见却令人烦恼的现象。最近，我与几位合作者开展了一系列研究，旨在探讨当人们不确定是否接受邀请时，他们的心里在想些什么。

paragraphs.contentEn: Social invitations can be a delicate dance, and people often misread what someone extending an invite wants to hear. We consistently found that people overestimate an inviter’s likelihood of preferring a “maybe” over a “no.” Moreover, they fail to realize how much more disrespected people feel when they receive a “maybe” in response to their invitation. Another pattern emerged: The more someone incorrectly assumed that a host preferred a tentative response, the more likely they were to respond with a “maybe” themselves.
paragraphs.contentZh: 社交邀请有时就像一场微妙的博弈，人们常常会误解邀请者真正希望听到的回应。我们的研究有个很一致的发现，即人们普遍高估了邀请者更倾向于听到“可能”而非“拒绝”的可能性。不仅如此，许多人也未意识到，“可能”的回复往往更容易让邀请者感到自己被怠慢。研究还揭示出另一种模式：一个人越是错误地认为邀请方更愿意听到模棱两可的回复，他自己就越可能回应一句“可能”。

paragraphs.contentEn: Naturally, we wanted to figure out why this awkward dynamic plays out. We found that it’s largely due to something called “motivated reasoning.” Motivated reasoning occurs when a person interprets information in a biased way to arrive at a conclusion that aligns with their own wishes. In other words, invitees convince themselves that inviters want to hear “maybe” instead of “no,” because a “maybe” is better for the invitee, allowing them to leave their options open. Saying “no” right off the bat eliminates one’s options and opens the door for FOMO, or fear of missing out, to emerge.
paragraphs.contentZh: 我们随即想弄清楚，这种尴尬的互动为什么会发生。我们发现，其背后主要源于一种被称为“动机性推理”的心理现象。所谓动机性推理，是指人们为了得出符合自身愿望的结论，而带有偏见地去解读信息。换句话说，因为“可能”的回复对受邀者更有利，能够继续保留选择的余地，因此他们会说服自己相信，邀请者宁可听到一句“可能吧”，也不想直接被拒绝。如果一开始就说“不”，不仅会立刻切断其他可能性，还可能会引发“错失恐惧症”（FOMO, a fear of missing out）。

paragraphs.contentEn: That said, there were certain situations that made people more comfortable saying “no” to an invite. In one study, we had recipients of an invitation put themselves in the shoes of the person extending the invite. This made them more likely to realize that they’d probably prefer a definitive answer. That is, it seemed to prevent motivated reasoning from emerging. In another study, we had participants get invited to do something they didn’t want to do. We found that motivated reasoning then became irrelevant: They had no desire to keep their options open, so they were more likely to assume that a “no” was preferable to a “maybe.”
paragraphs.contentZh: 话虽如此，我们也发现，在某些情境中人们其实更倾向于直接拒绝邀请。在一项研究中，我们让受邀者尝试站在邀请者的角度思考。结果发现，通过换位思考，他们更容易意识到对方可能更希望得到一个明确的答复。也就是说，这种视角的转换似乎抑制了动机性推理的出现。在另一项研究中，我们让参与者回应一个他们本身就不愿意参加的活动邀请。结果发现，此时动机性推理不再起作用：由于他们无意保留选择余地，因此更容易认为直接说“不”比回复“可能吧”更为妥当。

paragraphs.contentEn: Interestingly, while invitations are a widespread aspect of social life, social scientists have only recently started studying them. For example, a 2024 study found that people tend to overestimate the negative consequences of saying “no” to invitations. They think it will upset, anger and disappoint inviters more than is the case. This could also be part of the reason that many people fail to realize that someone extending an invitation prefers a “no” to a “maybe.”
paragraphs.contentZh: 有意思的一点是，尽管邀请是社交生活中无处不在的一环，但直到最近，社会科学家才开始研究这一现象。例如，2024年的一项研究发现，人们倾向于高估拒绝邀请所带来的负面影响。他们认为拒绝会让邀请者更加难过、生气或失望，但实际情况往往并非如此。这一点或许也能解释，为什么许多人没有意识到，对邀请者来说，明确的“不”比一句“再说吧”更易接受。

paragraphs.contentEn: Other research has explored whether people respond better to some reasons for declining an invite over others: saying you’re too busy, not great; saying you don’t have enough money to make it work, much better. While navigating social situations can be tricky, our work suggests that being direct and definitive is sometimes best. It might reduce your options. But it’ll keep those who invited you from being left in limbo – and maybe they’ll still think of you when the next concert comes to town.
paragraphs.contentZh: 其他研究还探讨了人们在拒绝邀请时，对不同理由的反应是否有所差别，结果发现：说自己太忙的效果并不好；而如果说自己经济上不太宽裕，暂时去不了，反而更容易让对方理解和接受。社交场合中的回应本就令人犯难，但我们的研究表明，有时候最好的做法是直接而明确。这样的回应或许会减少我们的选择余地，却能避免让邀请者陷入尴尬的等待——而且如果下次再有演唱会门票，他们可能依然愿意邀请你。
